say: Welcome to our last lesson, inquirers! Two parts today. First a challenge round with puzzles from all nine lessons. Then you become the puzzle maker: you build a small program that sets a maths puzzle, and you show it to the group.
Our rule all program long: notice it, test it, explain why. Today you do all three in front of an audience.

“Ten lessons ago you predicted the 100th term of a pattern and checked it in code. Today you built your own puzzle program and explained the maths to an audience. That is what inquirers do. Here is your certificate. Keep noticing, keep testing, and keep asking why!”

p6l10-title.note: Objective: Use ideas from all nine lessons (sequences, primes, negative numbers, algebra, counting, probability, angles, clock arithmetic, averages) in a mixed challenge round, then plan, build, test and present a small puzzle program, working out the maths by hand first and explaining why it works. Materials: Laptop or desktop with Scratch 3 (scratch.mit.edu), workbook (challenge round on page 1, planning sheet on page 2), pencil, mini whiteboard, the starter projects as .sb3 files (L10A_Mystery_Machine.sb3, L10B_Prime_or_Not.sb3, L10C_Lucky_Seven.sb3, L10D_Clock_Jumper.sb3; children use File, Load from your computer; each one already works, children change one thing), or build them from the slides, certificates, stamps. Online: Challenge round in teams of 2 in breakout rooms. Building: everyone in the main room with cameras on, asking for help in the chat. Showcase: in two rounds of 4, each child shares their screen for 2 minutes 15 seconds; the audience TYPES two stars and a question for each presenter in the chat (stars are typed, not spoken). A child may show a screenshot and the tutor runs the file. Children may paste a screenshot into the chat instead and the tutor runs their file, which removes screen-share switching. Block colours on our slides are simplified; in Scratch, find blocks by the category name on the left, not by colour. Time plan (this lesson changes the usual routine; no relay and no separate talk time): opening 0 to 2, sneak-peek puzzles 2 to 6, challenge round 6 to 19.5 (workbook page 1 in teams of 2, Q1 and Q3; check together; ask how we started as the first line of the check), starter projects 19.5 to 26.5 (only Starter A is run live; click to reveal), brain break 26.5 to 30, plan and build 30 to 58 (teaching for the planning sheet, then workbook page 2 and Scratch; Think harder and Go further are open to everyone), flex 58 to 60.5 (unscripted, lost first), showcase 60.5 to 82.5 (two rounds of 4, 2 minutes 15 seconds each plus a 20-second switch, stars typed in the chat, rubric in the showcase notes), exit slip with the talk question 82.5 to 86, looking back 86 to 88, certificates (sent as PDFs) and the last stamp 88 to 90. Build target: a working copy of one starter with ONE change is full marks; an own idea is optional. Children chose their starter and their twist at the end of Lesson 9. Before the lesson: build the starter projects once (A Mystery Machine, B Prime or Not?, C Lucky Seven and D Clock Jumper) and share them as .sb3 files (children use File, Load from your computer; no account needed) with shared project links as a backup. Print or fill in certificates, and decide a random showcase order. Showcase switching: ask the next child to have their screen ready while the one before answers questions; a child may paste a screenshot of the program into the chat and the tutor runs their file, which removes the switching time. SPINE: Today you choose the tool. Point at the row of eight tools on page 1 of the workbook.

p6l10-check.note: Minutes 2 to 6. These are ideas we have not learnt yet: say so, and say that guessing and "I do not know" are welcome and nobody is marked. Read the two puzzles aloud. Puzzle 1 is an access puzzle: any child can try it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone can get a first win. Puzzle 2 is a thinking puzzle on today's idea. ONE check moment only: after both puzzles, everyone says the answers together on three (nothing is held up to the camera). Never private chat. Never compare answers across children, never read wrong answers aloud. Then click to reveal the answers one after the other and move on with no reaction round: say each answer in 15 words or fewer, then say: "Both of these are what we learn today." Answers: Puzzle 1: 24, 29 and 34. Any child can count on. Puzzle 2: No. Every number in the list ends in 4 or 9 (it is 1 less than a multiple of 5), and 2026 ends in 6. A guess is welcome; today’s challenge round uses ideas like this. Invite the WHOLE group, never one child: say "When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Nobody is singled out. Any child can choose it and any child can go back. Never announce who is on which page and never say advanced or top group. Do not record this as a mark. Do not split a pair unless both children agree.

p6l10-explore1.note: Minutes 6 to 19.5 (this slide 6 to 8.5). Teams do Q1 and Q3; Q2 (prime hunters) is the take-home question, marked with a star in the workbook. Explain the rules, then send teams of 2 to breakout rooms (or work side by side). Points: 1 for each correct answer, 1 for each check (worked a different way, or tested in code), 1 for each reason they can say aloud. Each team keeps its own score on page 1 and shows it only if the team wants to: no tally on the board or in the chat. The point of the check and reason columns: a lucky guess is worth only a third of the points. Predict first: Look at the puzzles on page 1. Which one do you think will be hardest? Which lesson does each one come from? Write your guesses at the top of the page. Go further what-if (not a slide: paste it in the chat for any pair that finishes early, and take it up only if a pair wants to share): What if the hexagon puzzle used PENTAGONS joined along one side? Find the rule for the sticks and say how many pentagons use 101 sticks. Answer: 4n + 1 sticks (a pentagon needs 5 sticks and each new one adds 4). 101 sticks: 4n + 1 = 101, so n = 25 pentagons.

p6l10-ws1.note: Minutes 8.5 to 16.5. Show this preview, do not read it aloud. Visit each team. Ask "How did you start?" and "What is your check?" before giving any help. Hints: Stuck on a puzzle: which lesson does it remind you of? Make a table, list it in order, or draw it. Got an answer: earn the check point. Check it a different way, or test it in code. If a pair wants more: write a rule for Q1 that would make 2027 sticks. Is it possible with hexagons? Teams who finish early can test Q1 in Scratch (the four blocks are on the page) or list the Q3e numbers with two nested loops.

p6l10-ws1ans.note: Minutes 16.5 to 19.5. All the answers are shown at once. Children mark in a different colour (about 35 seconds a question). There is no separate how-we-started slide: ask it as the first line, "How did you start the hexagon puzzle?" (Make a table of hexagons and sticks; notice + 5 each time; the rule is 5n + 1.) Then ask ONE volunteer to explain only Q1. Q2 is the take-home question: its answer is here so children can mark it at home. Q1: each new hexagon adds 5 sticks (it shares one side), so 5n + 1; 5 × 10 + 1 = 51; 5n + 1 = 101 gives n = 20; the code starts at 6 and adds 5 fourteen times: 6 + 70 = 76, which is 5 × 15 + 1, the chain of 15. Q2: a 2-digit number with exactly 3 factors is the square of a prime: 25 or 49; digits add to 13: 49. 84 = 2 × 42 = 2 × 2 × 21 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 7. For 40 test every prime up to 20: 3 + 37, 11 + 29, 17 + 23 work; 2, 5, 7, 13, 19 do not (38, 35, 33, 27, 21 are not prime). Q3: a) −4 + 9 = 5, 5 − 12 = −7. b) 3n − 10 = n, so 2n = 10, n = 5 (or trial: 5 × 3 − 10 = 5). c) 360 ÷ 24 = 15. d) 100 hours = 8 × 12 + 4, so 4 hours on from 9: 1 o’clock. (Digit cards and probability are now in Think harder 4.)

p6l10-teach1.note: Minutes 19.5 to 21. Teach. Click each card. Say: "A program that shows an answer you could not check is not a puzzle, it is a mystery box. So the maths always comes first." Then the three starters, each about one minute. Children do not copy them yet: they choose one at the planning stage after the break.

p6l10-we1.note:
Minutes 21 to 23.5. Starter A (Lesson 4 idea). Run it on screen. Think-aloud: “Mystery Machine: the program picks n, works out 3n + 4 and shows it. If it shows 19, I go backwards: 19 − 4 = 15, 15 ÷ 3 = 5. Before I trust the program, I test it with a number I already know: if n is 5 it must show 19.” Note: Scratch uses * for ×. "answer" is what the player typed. The worksheet (Q4a) asks for a different test, n = 9, so do not reveal it. 7 blocks. Python version (optional):
import random
n = random.randint(1, 20)
out = n * 3 + 4
print("My machine does x 3, then + 4.")
print("Out came", out)
guess = int(input("What went in? "))
if guess == n:
 print("You cracked it!")
else:
 print("No, it was", n)
With n = 5 it prints "Out came 19"; typing 5 gives "You cracked it!", typing 7 gives "No, it was 5".

p6l10-we3.note:
Minutes 24.5 to 25.5. Starter C (Lesson 6 idea): one line only, NOT run live; children run it when they load the file. Think-aloud: “Lucky Seven: there are 6 × 6 = 36 equally likely results for two dice. 1 + 6, 2 + 5, 3 + 4, 4 + 3, 5 + 2, 6 + 1 make 7: that is 6 of 36, one sixth. So in 1000 rolls I expect about 167. When I run it I got 152, then 182, then 162: close to 167 but never the same, because the rolls are random.” The table: there are 6 × 6 = 36 ways two dice can land, all equally likely; the yellow cells (1 + 6, 2 + 5, … , 6 + 1) make 7. Run it 3 times on screen and write the results: they will differ. A run of 1000 usually lands between about 145 and 190. Worksheet Q4c asks about 8s, so do not count the 8s now. 5 blocks. Twist ideas: let the player pick the total; count every total in a list; compare 100 rolls with 10 000 rolls. Python version (optional):
import random
sevens = 0
for roll in range(1000):
 if random.randint(1, 6) + random.randint(1, 6) == 7:
 sevens = sevens + 1
print(sevens, "sevens in 1000 rolls")
print("We expect about", round(1000 / 6))
Three test runs printed 152, 182 and 162 sevens; the last line always prints "We expect about 167".

p6l10-key.note: Minutes 25.5 to 26.5. Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for while children build: (1) Coding before working out the maths, so there is no way to tell whether the output is right. (2) Testing only once, or only with the value the program happened to show, instead of a value worked out by hand (and an edge case such as 1 or 0). (3) Showcase: reading the code block by block instead of explaining the maths puzzle and why the program works.

p6l10-break.note: Minutes 26.5 to 30. 3.5 minutes. Call: square (4 turns of 90°), triangle (3 of 120°), hexagon (6 of 60°), then the surprise: a star (5 turns of 144°, which takes 2 full turns to face the front again). Online: children stay in view of the camera.

p6l10-teachplan.note:
Minutes 30 to 32.5. Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q5 is the planning table, Q6 the blocks and tests). Walk through a FOURTH idea so the starters stay fresh. Think-aloud: "My puzzle: 9 o’clock plus h hours. By hand: 9 + 5 = 14, take away 12: 2 o’clock. 9 + 15 = 24, take away two 12s: 0, which on a clock is 12. 9 + 30 = 39, take away three 12s: 3. I write these tests BEFORE I run anything." Click the rows. Then: "I found a bug with the edge case: without the if block it said 0 o’clock." Python version (optional):
hours = int(input("How many hours from 9 o'clock? "))
t = (9 + hours) % 12
if t == 0:
 t = 12
print(t, "o'clock")
Tested: 5 → "2 o'clock", 15 → "12 o'clock", 30 → "3 o'clock".

p6l10-teachtest.note: Minutes 32.5 to 33.5. Teach before worksheet page 2. Click each kind of test. Ask: "Why is 1 a good edge case for Prime or Not?" (it is the only whole number with exactly 1 factor; a program that counts badly might call it prime). "If Lucky Seven said 400, what would you think?" (a bug: 400 is far too many; maybe it counts 7 OR something, or never resets sevens to 0).

p6l10-ws2.note: Minutes 33.5 to 56. Show this preview, do not read it aloud. Q4: only the part for the starter you picked (about 2 minutes); Q5: three cells (idea, answer, twist); Q6: three test rows written BEFORE running. Then build for about 20 minutes (test as you go; a working copy of one starter with one change is full marks). Anyone who wants to start from their own idea may, but only after a starter works. Circulate: Ask: “What answer should your program give for this input? How do you know?” Ask: “What happens with an edge case: 1, 0, or the biggest number?” Ask: “In one sentence, what maths is your program about?” Hints: Hint 1: “Start from a starter project and change one thing: the rule, the numbers, or the question.” Hint 2: “Write the maths on your planning sheet first. Then find one block for each line of your plan.” Hint 3: “If the program disagrees with you, trace it in a table: which value goes in, what does each block do?” Anyone stuck after 5 minutes: build a starter exactly, then change ONE thing (the rule, the range, the total).

p6l10-ws2ans.note: Minutes 56 to 58. All the answers are shown at once. a) 9 × 3 + 4 = 31; (58 − 4) ÷ 3 = 18. b) 91 = 7 × 13, so it has 4 factors. c) 2 + 6, 3 + 5, 4 + 4, 5 + 3, 6 + 2: 5 of the 36 results; 1000 × 5 ÷ 36 is about 139 (138.9), and a real run will be near this, not exactly. Finish and save. Everyone gets their project open and ready to share.

p6l10-stretch.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some children are working, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. For children who finish building early. Answers: 1) 203 (nth term 4n + 3: 4 × 50 + 3). 2) 4: 4, 9, 25 and 49 (the squares of the primes 2, 3, 5, 7; their only factors are 1, the prime and the square). 3) 15/36 = 5/12 (prime totals: 2 in 1 way, 3 in 2, 5 in 4, 7 in 6, 11 in 2; 1 + 2 + 4 + 6 + 2 = 15). Each one can be tested in code: a loop for 1, a factor counter for 2, a dice simulation for 3.

p6l10-challenge.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some children are working, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Pair challenge for anyone who wants more, or take home. Ask for the reason every time. Answers: 1) 33 (multiples of 2: 50, of 3: 33, of both (6): 16; 100 − (50 + 33 − 16) = 33) 2) 4 (4 × 3 − 8 = 4). With + 8 it is −4 (−4 × 3 + 8 = −4).

p6l10-chdiag.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some children are working, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Show after pairs have tried the Challenge, or if they are stuck. The diagrams show the problem, not the answer. Ask: What do you notice? What repeats? What do we know? Answers are in the Challenge slide notes.

p6l10-chwalk.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some children are working, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Use after pairs have tried, with the "see it" slide. Q1 can be checked in code: repeat 100 with if (n mod 2 > 0) and (n mod 3 > 0) then change count by 1: it says 33. Q2 is the equation 3n − 8 = n from Lesson 4; the second part needs Lesson 3’s negative numbers. Trial in a table also works: n = 1, 2, 3, 4 gives OUT −5, −2, 1, 4.

p6l10-gap-pack.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it while some pairs are working or have finished, or use it live as an extra warm-up or tutor-bank question; never at a fixed minute, and it never takes time from the plan. ADDED ITEM pack (a slide-only addition for the skill gap "The greatest total you cannot make"; it is not in the printed workbook). TOOL: Make a table. SAY: Write the numbers 1 to 40 in rows of 4. Mark every total you can make. Look for the first row where every number is marked. ASK: Once you have 4 totals in a row, what happens next? How do you know 23 is the last one? LISTEN FOR: Four in a row is enough because adding 4 reaches everything after. 24 to 27 are all buyable (24 = 4 × 6, 25 = 16 + 9, 26 = 8 + 18, 27 = 3 × 9), so nothing above 23 is missing, and 23 cannot be made. Listen for the argument. Everyone writes the answer on their own paper, then say the answer together on three, then click the answer box. Nobody holds anything up, nobody is marked, and passing is always fine. ANSWER: 23 stickers. WHY: Totals are 4a + 9b. 24, 25, 26 and 27 can all be made, so every number from 24 up can be made by adding 4s. 23 cannot: 23 − 9 = 14, 23 − 18 = 5 are not multiples of 4, and 23 is not a multiple of 4. The greatest total that cannot be made is 23. SAME SKILL, NEW NUMBERS (tutor bank, say it aloud or write it on the board): Sheets come in 5s and 6s. What is the greatest total you cannot make? Answer: 19.

p6l10-showcase.note: Minutes 60.5 to 82.5. TWO ROUNDS OF 4 so nobody waits more than about 11 minutes: round 1 is about minutes 60.5 to 71.5, round 2 about 71.5 to 82.5. Each child has 2 minutes 15 seconds (show the puzzle 25 s, run it 30 s, prove it with one hand-worked test 35 s, explain the maths 45 s) plus a 20-second switch: 8 x 2:35 = 20 minutes 40 seconds, plus set-up (the flex minutes before the showcase are for this). Stars (two stars and a question) are TYPED in the chat by the audience, not spoken, so a spoken reply never breaks the slot. A child who is not ready can show a screenshot and you run their file, or show their plan only. Use a timer, volunteers first (never name a child to go next); a child may pass to the second round. The next child has their screen ready while the one before answers questions; a child may paste a screenshot into the chat and the tutor runs their file instead of sharing a screen. A child who did not finish shows their plan and the tests they worked out by hand: that still earns full marks for maths and testing. SHOWCASE RUBRIC (1 to 3 points each; note it privately, share only the stars and the wish). Maths: 1 = gives an answer; 2 = correct answer with working; 3 = correct, and can say why the rule works. Testing: 1 = ran it once; 2 = a test with an answer known in advance; 3 = a known-answer test and an edge case, or a bug found and fixed. Code: 1 = it runs; 2 = under 15 blocks with sensible variable names; 3 = a twist that changes the puzzle (new rule, score, levels). Explaining: 1 = reads the blocks aloud; 2 = says what the program does; 3 = explains the maths and answers a question from the group. Questions to ask each presenter: "Which test did you do first?" "What would happen with 0 or 1?" "Where is the maths in your blocks?" Write one specific sentence of praise for each child for the certificate moment.

p6l10-exit.note: Minutes 82.5 to 86. The talk question is folded into the exit slip as its last line (there is no separate talk time): "What was the hardest bug you fixed today? How did you find it?" Everyone ticks the slip against the answer slide. Open. Look for a test worked out by hand before running the program, and a correct maths reason. Extension to take home: Level up your program: ask 5 questions and keep a score, let the player choose the rule, or count every dice total in a list. Write a Python version and check it gives the same results.

p6l10-reflect.note: SPINE: Minutes 86 to 88. Start the timer (75 seconds). Say: "Pick one problem from today. Question 1: did I answer the question? Question 2: does my answer make sense? Question 3: can I check it another way? Tick, write one line, or pass. If you are still stuck, tick the box and I will come." Children tick the Look back box on the Choose and look-back page of their workbook, or just tick on paper. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out; the tutor may look at it afterwards. If a child ticks "I am still stuck", check in during the open session next lesson (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby; never a direct message). Do not ask children to share. Praise a check you saw, not speed. Then stamp the journals. After the look-back, minutes 88 to 90 are flex time (the buffer): finish stamps, then goodbye. Do not start anything new.

p6l10-end.note: Minutes 88 to 90. Certificates are sent to parents as a PDF with one specific line of praise already written for each child (the showcase rubric asks for it): do not hand out paper certificates or write praise live. Say one sentence of praise to the whole group. “Ten lessons ago you predicted the 100th term of a pattern and checked it in code. Today you built your own puzzle program and explained the maths to an audience. That is what inquirers do. Here is your certificate. Keep noticing, keep testing, and keep asking why!” Ask each child to name one puzzle or program they enjoyed. Give parents the one-page summary from the tutor guide, with links to Scratch and to the starter projects so children can keep building.
